diagrams.title: Production possibilities curve (PPC)
diagrams.summary: The maximum combinations of two goods an economy can produce with all its resources fully and efficiently employed.
steps: The PPC shows every maximum combination of Good X and Good Y the economy can produce when all its resources are fully and efficiently employed, with a given state of technology.
Points on the curve such as A and B are productively efficient. A point inside the curve such as C means resources are unemployed or used inefficiently.
A point outside the curve such as D is unattainable with the current quantity and quality of resources — this is scarcity.

Moving from A to B gains ΔX but gives up ΔY: the opportunity cost of the extra X. The curve is concave (bowed out) because resources are not equally suited to both goods, so opportunity cost increases.
examTips: Label both axes with the goods, not "price" and "quantity".
A straight-line PPC means constant opportunity cost; concave means increasing opportunity cost.

diagrams.title: PPC: actual and potential growth
diagrams.summary: Actual growth uses idle resources (a move towards the PPC); potential growth increases capacity (an outward shift).
steps: PPC₁ shows the economy's current productive capacity.
At A some resources are unemployed. Reducing unemployment moves the economy from A towards B on the PPC: actual economic growth (more real output from existing capacity).
An increase in the quantity or quality of factors of production (e.g. investment in capital, education, new technology) shifts the PPC outward to PPC₂: potential economic growth.
Points such as C, unattainable before, can now be produced. Producing more capital goods today (at the cost of consumer goods) shifts the PPC out further in the future.
examTips: Actual growth = movement towards the curve; potential growth = shift of the curve.
An improvement in technology for only one good pivots the PPC along that axis.

diagrams.title: Circular flow of income
diagrams.summary: Money flows between households and firms, with leakages (S, T, M) leaving the flow and injections (I, G, X) entering it.

notes.text: Equilibrium: I + G + X = S + T + M

steps: In a simple two-sector model, households sell factor services to firms and receive factor incomes; they spend this income on firms' goods and services. Income = expenditure = output.
Leakages (withdrawals) are income not passed on as spending on domestic output: savings, taxes and imports. They reduce the size of the flow.
Injections are spending that does not come from households' incomes: investment, government spending and exports. They increase the size of the flow.
National income is in equilibrium when total injections equal total leakages. If injections exceed leakages national income rises; if leakages exceed injections it falls.
examTips: Name the sector each leakage goes to and each injection comes from.
This is the basis of the three equivalent ways of measuring GDP.

diagrams.title: Demand: movement along vs shift
diagrams.summary: A change in the good's own price moves along the demand curve; a change in any other determinant shifts it.
steps: The demand curve slopes downward: ceteris paribus, as price falls quantity demanded rises (law of demand).
A fall in price from P₁ to P₂ causes a movement along the curve from a to b — an increase in quantity demanded (extension).

A change in a non-price determinant (income, prices of substitutes or complements, tastes, expectations, number of consumers) shifts the whole curve. Here demand increases from D₁ to D₂: more is demanded at every price.
examTips: "Increase in demand" = shift; "increase in quantity demanded" = movement.
A decrease in demand shifts the curve to the left.

diagrams.title: Supply: movement along vs shift
diagrams.summary: A change in the good's own price moves along the supply curve; a change in costs, technology, taxes etc. shifts it.
steps: The supply curve slopes upward: ceteris paribus, a higher price gives firms an incentive to supply more (law of supply), as higher prices cover rising marginal costs.
A rise in price from P₁ to P₂ causes a movement along the curve from a to b — an increase in quantity supplied.
A change in a non-price determinant (costs of factors, technology, indirect taxes, subsidies, expectations, number of firms) shifts the curve. Lower costs shift supply right from S₁ to S₂.
examTips: An indirect tax shifts supply up/left; a subsidy shifts it down/right.

diagrams.title: Market equilibrium, excess demand and excess supply
diagrams.summary: Equilibrium is where quantity demanded equals quantity supplied; any other price creates a surplus or shortage that the price mechanism removes.
steps: Equilibrium is at e, where quantity demanded equals quantity supplied: the market clears at price Pe and quantity Qe.
At P₁ above equilibrium, quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded: excess supply (a surplus). Firms cut prices to sell stock, so price falls towards Pe.
At P₂ below equilibrium, quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied: excess demand (a shortage). Price is bid up, signalling firms to supply more and rationing consumers, until Pe is reached.
examTips: Always label the excess as a horizontal distance between Qd and Qs.

diagrams.title: Increase in demand: new equilibrium
diagrams.summary: An increase in demand raises both equilibrium price and quantity.
steps: The market begins in equilibrium at e₁ with price P₁ and quantity Q₁.
A non-price determinant changes (e.g. incomes rise for a normal good), so demand shifts right from D₁ to D₂. At the old price P₁ there is now excess demand.
The shortage pushes price up, which signals firms to raise quantity supplied (a movement along S). The new equilibrium is e₂: price rises to P₂ and quantity rises to Q₂.
examTips: Price rises AND quantity rises — both changes must be labelled on the axes.

diagrams.title: Increase in supply: new equilibrium
diagrams.summary: An increase in supply lowers equilibrium price and raises equilibrium quantity.
steps: The market begins in equilibrium at e₁.
A fall in costs of production (or better technology, or a subsidy) shifts supply right from S₁ to S₂. At the old price P₁ there is excess supply.
Firms lower prices to sell the surplus, and quantity demanded extends. The new equilibrium is e₂: price falls to P₂ and quantity rises to Q₂.

diagrams.title: Consumer surplus, producer surplus and allocative efficiency
diagrams.summary: At the competitive equilibrium social surplus (CS + PS) is maximised, so resources are allocatively efficient.
steps: The competitive market is in equilibrium at e. The demand curve shows marginal benefit to consumers; the supply curve shows marginal cost to producers.
Consumer surplus is the difference between what consumers are willing and able to pay (the demand curve) and the price they actually pay, summed over all units bought.
Producer surplus is the difference between the price producers receive and the lowest price they would accept (the supply curve), summed over all units sold.
Social (community) surplus = CS + PS. It is maximised at Qe, where MSB = MSC: allocative efficiency. Producing more or less than Qe would reduce social surplus — a welfare loss.
examTips: When there are no externalities, D = MPB = MSB and S = MPC = MSC.

diagrams.title: PED: perfectly inelastic, perfectly elastic and unit elastic
diagrams.summary: The special cases of price elasticity of demand and how each is drawn.
steps: Perfectly inelastic demand (PED = 0): a vertical curve. Quantity demanded does not change at all when price changes.
Perfectly elastic demand (PED = ∞): a horizontal curve. Any rise in price above this level causes quantity demanded to fall to zero — the demand faced by a firm in perfect competition.
Unit elastic demand (PED = 1): a rectangular hyperbola. The percentage change in quantity always equals the percentage change in price, so total revenue (P × Q) is the same at every point.
examTips: Between these: 0 < PED < 1 is inelastic, PED > 1 is elastic — PED is quoted as an absolute value.

diagrams.title: PED and total revenue: elastic demand
diagrams.summary: When demand is price elastic, a price cut raises total revenue.
steps: At price P₁ the firm sells Q₁; total revenue is P₁ × Q₁.
The firm cuts its price to P₂. Because demand is price elastic, quantity demanded rises by a larger percentage than the fall in price.
The firm loses revenue on the units it was already selling: (P₁ − P₂) × Q₁.
It gains revenue on the extra units sold: (Q₂ − Q₁) × P₂. The gain exceeds the loss, so total revenue rises. Raising price would reduce TR.
examTips: Elastic: price and TR move in opposite directions.

diagrams.title: PED and total revenue: inelastic demand
diagrams.summary: When demand is price inelastic, a price rise raises total revenue.
steps: At price P₁ the firm sells Q₁; total revenue is P₁ × Q₁.
The firm raises its price to P₂. Because demand is price inelastic, quantity demanded falls by a smaller percentage than the rise in price.
Revenue gained on the units still sold: (P₂ − P₁) × Q₂.
Revenue lost on units no longer sold: (Q₁ − Q₂) × P₁ — a thin strip. The gain is larger, so total revenue rises. This is why governments tax goods with inelastic demand.
examTips: Inelastic: price and TR move in the same direction.

diagrams.title: PED along a linear demand curve
diagrams.summary: A straight-line demand curve has constant slope but its elasticity changes along its length.
steps: The slope (ΔP/ΔQ) is the same everywhere on a straight line, but PED = (ΔQ/ΔP) × (P/Q) also depends on the ratio P/Q, which changes along the curve.
Near the top, P is high and Q is low, so a given change in quantity is a large percentage change: demand is price elastic. Lowering price here raises TR.
At the midpoint PED = 1 and total revenue is at its maximum.
Below the midpoint P is low and Q is high, so demand is price inelastic. Lowering price here reduces TR.
examTips: Never say a steep curve "is" inelastic without qualification — elasticity is measured at a point or over a range.

diagrams.title: PES: perfectly inelastic, perfectly elastic and unit elastic supply
diagrams.summary: The special cases of price elasticity of supply.
steps: Perfectly inelastic supply (PES = 0): a vertical curve. Quantity supplied is fixed whatever the price, e.g. seats in a stadium in the short run.
Perfectly elastic supply (PES = ∞): a horizontal curve. Producers supply any quantity at this price — e.g. world supply to a small importing country.
Unit elastic supply (PES = 1): any straight line through the origin, whatever its slope.

diagrams.title: PES along linear supply curves
diagrams.summary: Where a straight-line supply curve meets the axes tells you whether it is elastic, unit elastic or inelastic.
steps: A straight-line supply curve through the origin has PES = 1 at every point.
A straight-line supply curve that cuts the price axis has PES > 1 (elastic) at every point, though PES falls towards 1 as output rises.
A straight-line supply curve that cuts the quantity axis has PES < 1 (inelastic) at every point.

diagrams.title: Price volatility of primary commodities
diagrams.summary: Low PED and low PES mean a supply shock causes a large change in price but a small change in quantity.
steps: Demand for primary commodities (food, raw materials) is price inelastic: they are necessities with few substitutes. Supply is price inelastic because of long production times and perishability.
A supply shock — e.g. a poor harvest caused by drought — shifts supply left from S₁ to S₂.
Because both curves are steep, price rises sharply from P₁ to P₂ while quantity falls only a little. Prices and producer incomes are volatile, which harms commodity-dependent economies.
examTips: Link to commodity dependence as a barrier to development and to HL terms of trade.

diagrams.title: Price ceiling (maximum price)
diagrams.summary: A maximum price below equilibrium creates a shortage, a welfare loss and the risk of a parallel market.
steps: Without intervention the market clears at e, with price Pe and quantity Qe.
The government sets a maximum price Pmax below Pe (e.g. rent controls or food price caps). Quantity supplied falls to Qs and quantity demanded rises to Qd: a shortage (excess demand) of Qd − Qs.
Only Qs is now produced, below the allocatively efficient Qe. The lost social surplus between Qs and Qe is a welfare loss.
Consumers would be willing to pay Pb for the limited quantity Qs, so a parallel (black) market can arise. Non-price rationing (queues, waiting lists) also appears.
examTips: A ceiling must be set BELOW equilibrium to have any effect.
Stakeholders: consumers who buy gain; those who cannot buy lose; producers lose.

diagrams.title: Price floor (minimum price)
diagrams.summary: A minimum price above equilibrium creates a surplus that the government may have to buy.

elements.label: Government spending to buy the surplus

steps: Without intervention the market clears at e.
The government sets a minimum price Pmin above Pe (e.g. to support farmers' incomes). Quantity demanded falls to Qd while quantity supplied rises to Qs: a surplus (excess supply) of Qs − Qd.

To maintain the floor the government may buy the surplus, costing (Qs − Qd) × Pmin, with an opportunity cost for other spending. Storing or destroying the surplus is wasteful, and resources are over-allocated to the good.
examTips: A floor must be set ABOVE equilibrium to have any effect.

diagrams.title: Minimum wage
diagrams.summary: A minimum wage above the equilibrium wage creates a surplus of labour — unemployment.
steps: In a competitive labour market the wage is We and Qe workers are employed. Firms demand labour; households supply it.
A legal minimum wage Wmin is set above We. Firms demand only Qd workers, while Qs people want to work at that wage.
The surplus of labour Qs − Qd is unemployment. Those who keep jobs earn more, but some lose jobs; firms' costs rise.
examTips: In the labour market households are the sellers (supply) and firms the buyers (demand).

diagrams.title: Specific (per-unit) indirect tax
diagrams.summary: A specific tax shifts supply up by the amount of the tax, raising the price consumers pay and lowering the price producers keep.
steps: Before the tax the market is in equilibrium at e₁ (P₁, Q₁).
A specific tax is a fixed amount per unit. It raises firms' costs, so supply shifts vertically upward by the amount of the tax, parallel to the original curve, to S + tax.
The new equilibrium is e₂. Consumers now pay Pc; producers receive Pc minus the tax, i.e. Pp. Quantity falls from Q₁ to Q₂.
Government revenue = tax × Q₂ (the rectangle). The part above P₁ is paid by consumers, the part below by producers: the tax incidence.
Q₂ units are traded instead of Q₁, so the lost consumer and producer surplus not collected as revenue is a welfare loss.
examTips: The vertical distance between S and S + tax is the tax per unit — label it.
The more inelastic demand is, the greater the consumer share.

diagrams.title: Ad valorem (percentage) indirect tax
diagrams.summary: A percentage tax makes the supply curve pivot upward: the tax per unit grows as price rises.
steps: Before the tax the market is in equilibrium at e₁.
An ad valorem tax is a percentage of the price (e.g. VAT/GST). The tax per unit is larger at higher prices, so the new supply curve diverges from the original rather than shifting parallel.
Consumers pay Pc, producers keep Pp, and quantity falls to Q₂.
Tax revenue = (Pc − Pp) × Q₂. The triangle between Q₂ and Q₁ is the welfare loss.
examTips: Specific tax → parallel shift; ad valorem → pivot (diverging curves).

diagrams.title: Tax incidence when demand is price inelastic
diagrams.summary: With inelastic demand most of an indirect tax is passed on to consumers.
steps: Demand is price inelastic (steep), e.g. for cigarettes or petrol.
A specific tax shifts supply up by the tax. Because consumers barely reduce their purchases, price rises by most of the tax: from P₁ to Pc. Quantity falls only slightly.
The consumer share of the tax (Pc − P₁) × Q₂ is much larger than the producer share (P₁ − Pp) × Q₂. Revenue is high and the fall in output — and so the welfare loss — is small.
examTips: Incidence falls more heavily on whichever side of the market is less elastic.
If demand is elastic, producers bear most of the tax.

diagrams.title: Subsidy to producers
diagrams.summary: A per-unit subsidy shifts supply down, lowering the price consumers pay and raising the price producers receive.
steps: Before the subsidy the market is in equilibrium at e₁.
A per-unit subsidy lowers firms' costs, so supply shifts vertically down by the subsidy to S − subsidy.
At the new equilibrium e₂, consumers pay a lower price Pc, producers receive Pc plus the subsidy (Pp), and quantity rises to Q₂.
The government pays subsidy × Q₂ (the rectangle) — an opportunity cost of spending elsewhere.
In a market without externalities, producing Q₂ > Q₁ over-allocates resources: the triangle is a welfare loss.
examTips: Where there is a positive externality, a subsidy can instead remove a welfare loss — see the merit-good diagram.

diagrams.title: Negative externality of production
diagrams.summary: External costs mean MSC > MPC, so the free market over-produces and there is a welfare loss.
steps: The free market is in equilibrium at m, where MPB = MPC: price Pm and quantity Qm.
Production creates external costs for third parties (e.g. pollution), so the marginal social cost is above the marginal private cost. The vertical gap is the marginal external cost (MEC).
The socially optimal output is Q*, where MSB = MSC. The market produces too much: Qm > Q*, an over-allocation of resources, and price is too low.
For each unit between Q* and Qm, MSC exceeds MSB. The shaded triangle is the welfare loss.
examTips: Put the welfare loss triangle's point at the social optimum, pointing towards the market output.
Policies: Pigouvian/carbon tax, tradable permits, regulation.

diagrams.title: Negative externality of consumption (demerit good)
diagrams.summary: External costs of consumption mean MSB < MPB, so the free market over-consumes.
steps: The free market is in equilibrium at m, where MPB = MPC.
Consumption creates external costs for third parties (e.g. passive smoking, drink-driving), so the marginal social benefit is below the marginal private benefit.
The social optimum is Q*, where MSB = MSC. Consumption Qm is greater than Q*: over-consumption and over-allocation of resources.
Between Q* and Qm, MSC > MSB: the shaded triangle is the welfare loss.
examTips: Demerit goods are usually drawn this way; imperfect information also leads consumers to overvalue them.

diagrams.title: Positive externality of production
diagrams.summary: External benefits of production mean MSC < MPC, so the free market under-produces.
steps: The free market is in equilibrium at m, where MPB = MPC.
Production creates external benefits for third parties (e.g. firms training workers who later move to other firms, or R&D spillovers), so MSC lies below MPC.
The social optimum is Q*, where MSB = MSC. The market under-produces: Qm < Q*, an under-allocation of resources.
Between Qm and Q*, MSB > MSC, so society loses the shaded welfare.
examTips: Policies: subsidies to producers, direct government provision.

diagrams.title: Positive externality of consumption (merit good)
diagrams.summary: External benefits of consumption mean MSB > MPB, so the free market under-consumes.
steps: The free market is in equilibrium at m, where MPB = MPC.
Consumption creates external benefits for third parties (e.g. vaccinations, education), so MSB lies above MPB. Merit goods are also under-consumed because people underestimate their private benefits.
The social optimum is Q*, where MSB = MSC. Consumption Qm < Q*: under-consumption and under-allocation of resources.
Between Qm and Q*, MSB > MSC: the shaded triangle is the welfare loss.
examTips: Policies: subsidies, direct provision, advertising/education, legislation, nudges.

diagrams.title: Correcting a negative externality with a Pigouvian tax
diagrams.summary: A tax equal to the marginal external cost shifts MPC up to MSC, moving the market to the social optimum.
steps: Without intervention the market produces Qm, where MPB = MPC, but the social optimum is Q* where MSB = MSC. The triangle is the welfare loss from over-production.
The government imposes a tax per unit equal to the marginal external cost. Firms now face MPC + tax = MSC: the externality is internalised. Output falls to Q* and price rises to P*.
Producers keep Pp per unit; the government earns revenue that can fund clean-up or compensation. The welfare loss is removed — allocative efficiency is restored.
examTips: Evaluation: MEC is hard to measure in money; demand may be inelastic; firms may relocate; regressive effects.

diagrams.title: Tradable permits (cap and trade)
diagrams.summary: The government fixes the supply of permits; demand determines their price.
steps: The government sets a cap on total pollution and issues that many permits, so supply is perfectly inelastic at S₁. Demand from firms that pollute determines the permit price P₁.
If demand for permits rises (e.g. economic growth), the price rises to P₂ but pollution cannot rise above the cap.
Reducing the cap over time (S₂) raises the price further, giving firms a stronger incentive to invest in cleaner technology. Firms that cut pollution cheaply can sell spare permits.
examTips: Advantage over a tax: certainty about the quantity of pollution. Disadvantage: uncertain price and setting the right cap.

diagrams.title: Correcting under-consumption of a merit good with a subsidy
diagrams.summary: A subsidy equal to the marginal external benefit at Q* shifts supply down so the market reaches the social optimum.
steps: The market under-consumes: it produces Qm where MPB = MPC, but the optimum is at Q* where MSB = MSC.
The government pays producers a subsidy per unit equal to the external benefit at Q*, shifting supply down to S − subsidy.
The new market equilibrium n is at Q*: consumers pay the lower price Pc and consume the socially optimal quantity. Alternatives: direct provision, or advertising that shifts MPB towards MSB.
examTips: Evaluation: opportunity cost of government spending; difficulty measuring the external benefit; firms may become inefficient.

diagrams.title: Short-run cost curves
diagrams.summary: MC, AVC, AFC and ATC, and why MC cuts AVC and ATC at their lowest points.
steps: Marginal cost is the extra cost of one more unit. It falls at first, then rises because of the law of diminishing marginal returns: with a fixed factor, each extra worker adds less output.
AFC = TFC ÷ Q falls continuously as fixed costs are spread over more output. AVC is U-shaped, also because of diminishing returns.
ATC = AVC + AFC. The vertical gap between ATC and AVC is AFC, so it narrows as output rises.
MC cuts both AVC and ATC at their minimum points: when the marginal is below the average it pulls the average down, and when it is above it pulls the average up.
examTips: Draw MC through the lowest points of AVC and ATC — examiners check this.
Minimum ATC is the productively efficient output.

diagrams.title: Revenue curves: price taker vs price maker
diagrams.summary: A perfectly competitive firm faces P = AR = MR; a firm with market power faces downward-sloping AR with MR below it.

elements.text: MR falls twice as fast as AR

steps: A firm in perfect competition is a price taker: it can sell any quantity at the market price, so its demand curve is perfectly elastic and P = AR = MR.
A firm with market power must lower its price to sell more, so AR (its demand curve) slopes down. MR lies below AR because the lower price applies to all units, not just the extra one.
With a straight-line AR, MR has the same vertical intercept and twice the slope. MR = 0 where total revenue is at its maximum (the unit-elastic midpoint of AR).

diagrams.title: Perfect competition: short-run abnormal profit
diagrams.summary: The industry sets the price; the firm produces where MC = MR and earns abnormal profit if P > ATC.
steps: Market demand and supply determine the industry price Pe.
Each firm is a price taker: it can sell any output at Pe, so P = AR = MR is a horizontal line at Pe.
The firm maximises profit where MC = MR, producing q.
At q, price (AR) is above average total cost, so the firm earns abnormal profit = (P − ATC) × q, the shaded rectangle.
examTips: Firm output is lower-case q; industry output is Q.
This is short run only — the profit attracts new firms (see the long-run diagram).

diagrams.title: Perfect competition: short-run loss
diagrams.summary: If price is below ATC but above AVC, the firm makes a loss but keeps producing in the short run.
steps: Low market demand gives a low industry price Pe, which is below the firm's minimum ATC.
The firm produces where MC = MR at q (minimising its loss). Price is below ATC, so it makes a loss of (ATC − P) × q.
Price is still above AVC, so revenue covers all variable costs and part of fixed costs. The firm continues to produce in the short run; in the long run, if losses persist, firms leave the industry.
examTips: Short run: produce if P ≥ AVC. Long run: stay only if P ≥ ATC.

diagrams.title: Perfect competition: long-run equilibrium
diagrams.summary: Free entry removes abnormal profit: price falls to minimum ATC, so the firm is productively and allocatively efficient.
steps: Short-run abnormal profit at price P₁ signals profit opportunities. With no barriers to entry, new firms enter the industry.
Entry shifts industry supply right from S₁ to S₂, so price falls to P₂. Each firm's AR = MR line falls.
Entry stops when P = minimum ATC: firms earn only normal profit. At q₂, P = MC (allocatively efficient) and output is at minimum ATC (productively efficient).
examTips: Long-run PC equilibrium: P = AR = MR = MC = min ATC.
If firms make losses, exit shifts supply left until price rises back to min ATC.

diagrams.title: Break-even and shut-down price
diagrams.summary: Minimum ATC gives the break-even price; minimum AVC gives the short-run shut-down price.

elements.text: Firm's SR supply = MC above min AVC →

steps: The firm's cost curves. In perfect competition its price equals MR.
Break-even price = minimum ATC. At this price the firm earns exactly normal profit (zero economic profit). Above it, abnormal profit.
Shut-down price = minimum AVC. Below this price the firm cannot even cover its variable costs, so it shuts down in the short run (its loss is then only its fixed costs).
Between the two prices the firm makes a loss but stays open in the short run. The firm's short-run supply curve is its MC curve above minimum AVC.
examTips: Break-even: P = min ATC (long-run condition). Shut-down: P = min AVC (short-run condition).

diagrams.title: Monopoly: profit maximisation
diagrams.summary: The monopolist produces where MC = MR and charges the price on the demand curve, earning abnormal profit protected by barriers to entry.
steps: The monopolist is the industry, so it faces the downward-sloping market demand curve (AR). MR lies below AR.
Add the firm's cost curves, MC and ATC.
Profit is maximised where MC = MR, at output Qm. The price is read off the demand curve above Qm: Pm.
Because AR > ATC at Qm, the monopolist earns abnormal profit. High barriers to entry stop new firms entering, so the profit persists in the long run.
examTips: Go up from MC = MR to the demand curve for price — not across from MC = MR.

diagrams.title: Monopoly: welfare loss and inefficiency
diagrams.summary: Compared with the allocatively efficient output, a monopoly restricts output and raises price, causing a welfare loss.

elements.text: Not at min ATC: productively inefficient

steps: The monopolist produces Qm (where MC = MR) and charges Pm.
Allocative efficiency requires P = MC (MSB = MSC), at output Qa and price Pa. The monopoly under-produces and over-charges.
Units between Qm and Qa are valued by consumers (AR) more than they cost to produce (MC) but are not produced: the triangle is the welfare loss — a market failure caused by market power.
The monopolist also does not produce at minimum ATC, so it is productively inefficient. Possible offsets: economies of scale and abnormal profit funding R&D (dynamic efficiency).
examTips: Policies: competition law/merger control, price regulation, nationalisation, fines, trade liberalisation.

diagrams.title: Natural monopoly
diagrams.summary: Economies of scale are so large that LRAC is still falling where it meets market demand, so one firm can supply the market most cheaply.
steps: Huge fixed (infrastructure) costs mean LRAC falls over the whole relevant range of output — e.g. water, rail or electricity networks.
Market demand cuts LRAC while it is still falling. A single firm can produce any output more cheaply than two or more firms sharing the market.
An unregulated natural monopoly maximises profit at MC = MR, producing Qm at price Pm and earning abnormal profit.
Forcing allocative efficiency (P = MC at Qa) would leave price below average cost, so the firm would make a loss. Governments therefore regulate price (e.g. at AC), subsidise, or nationalise.

diagrams.title: Monopolistic competition: short run
diagrams.summary: Product differentiation gives a downward-sloping, fairly elastic demand curve and the chance of short-run abnormal profit.
steps: Each firm sells a differentiated product, so it has a little market power: its demand curve slopes down but is relatively elastic because there are many close substitutes.
The firm maximises profit where MC = MR, producing q and charging P from the demand curve.
In the short run P > ATC, so the firm earns abnormal profit. Because barriers to entry are low, this attracts new firms.

diagrams.title: Monopolistic competition: long run
diagrams.summary: Entry shifts each firm's demand left until it is tangent to ATC: normal profit, with excess capacity.
steps: New firms enter, attracted by short-run abnormal profit. Each existing firm loses customers, so its demand curve shifts left (and becomes more elastic).
Entry continues until the demand curve is tangent to ATC. Where MC = MR, P = ATC: firms earn only normal profit.

The firm produces below the output at minimum ATC — it has excess capacity and is not productively efficient. P > MC, so it is not allocatively efficient either; the benefit is greater consumer choice.
examTips: Draw AR just touching ATC directly above where MC = MR.

diagrams.title: Long-run average cost: economies and diseconomies of scale
diagrams.summary: LRAC falls with economies of scale, then rises with diseconomies of scale.
steps: In the long run all factors are variable, so the firm can change its scale of production. LRAC shows the lowest average cost of each output.
As scale increases, LRAC falls: economies of scale (e.g. specialisation, bulk buying, cheaper finance, better technology).
The output at which LRAC first reaches its minimum is the minimum efficient scale.
Beyond this, LRAC rises: diseconomies of scale from coordination, communication and motivation problems in large organisations.

diagrams.title: Game theory: the prisoner's dilemma in oligopoly
diagrams.summary: Each firm's dominant strategy is to cut price, even though both would earn more by colluding.

notes.text: Whatever B does, A earns more pricing low (14 > 10, 5 > 2).
Both cut prices and earn 5 each — worse than 10 each.
Collusion (a cartel) could keep 10 each, but each has an incentive to cheat.

steps: Two oligopolists each choose a high or a low price. Their profits depend on each other's choice: strategic interdependence.
Firm A reasons: if B prices high, A earns 14 with a low price vs 10 with a high price; if B prices low, A earns 5 vs 2. Low price is A's dominant strategy — and by symmetry, B's too.
Both choose low prices and earn 5 each — the Nash equilibrium. Neither can do better by changing strategy alone.
If they colluded and both priced high they would earn 10 each. This is why firms are tempted to form cartels — and why cartels are unstable: each firm gains by cheating.
examTips: Explain the reasoning for one firm, then state "by symmetry" for the other.

diagrams.title: The business cycle
diagrams.summary: Real GDP fluctuates around its long-term growth trend through expansion, peak, contraction and trough.
steps: The long-term growth trend shows the average growth of potential output over time.
Actual real GDP fluctuates around the trend in a repeated pattern.
During an expansion real GDP rises and unemployment falls, up to a peak. In a contraction real GDP falls; two consecutive quarters of negative growth is a recession, ending at a trough.
Above the trend there is a positive (inflationary) output gap — actual output exceeds potential. Below it there is a negative (deflationary) output gap with cyclical unemployment.
examTips: A fall in the growth rate is not a recession — real GDP must actually fall.

diagrams.title: Aggregate demand: shifts
diagrams.summary: AD slopes down; a change in any component (C, I, G, X − M) not caused by the price level shifts it.
steps: AD = C + I + G + (X − M): total planned spending on domestic output at each average price level. It slopes down because of the wealth, interest-rate and international-trade effects of a lower price level.
An increase in any component shifts AD right: e.g. higher consumer or business confidence, lower interest rates, higher government spending, a fall in the exchange rate or higher incomes abroad.
A fall in any component shifts AD left, e.g. higher income taxes, higher interest rates or a recession in trading partners.

diagrams.title: Short-run aggregate supply: shifts
diagrams.summary: SRAS slopes up; changes in firms' costs shift it.
steps: SRAS shows the total output firms plan to supply at each average price level in the short run, when wages and other factor prices are fixed. It slopes up because higher prices raise profitability.
An increase in costs — higher wages, higher raw material or energy prices, higher indirect taxes, a negative supply shock — shifts SRAS left (up).
A fall in costs — lower wages or commodity prices, subsidies to firms, a favourable supply shock — shifts SRAS right (down).

diagrams.title: Short-run macroeconomic equilibrium
diagrams.summary: Real GDP and the average price level are determined where AD = SRAS.
steps: Aggregate demand and short-run aggregate supply.
Short-run equilibrium is at e, where AD = SRAS: equilibrium real GDP Ye and average price level Pe. A shift in either curve changes both.

diagrams.title: Monetarist / New Classical long-run equilibrium
diagrams.summary: In the new classical model LRAS is vertical at potential output, and the economy settles where AD, SRAS and LRAS meet.
steps: Monetarists/new classical economists argue LRAS is vertical at potential output Yp, determined by the quantity and quality of factors of production — not by the price level.
In the short run, AD and SRAS determine output and prices.
Long-run equilibrium is where AD = SRAS on the LRAS curve: the economy produces Yp with unemployment at its natural rate. Because wages and prices are flexible, the economy returns here by itself.

diagrams.title: Keynesian AS curve
diagrams.summary: The Keynesian AS curve has a horizontal, an upward-sloping and a vertical section, so the effect of AD depends on spare capacity.
steps: Keynesians argue that wages and prices are sticky downward, and that the economy can operate with lots of spare capacity. AS becomes vertical only at full employment output Yf.
Horizontal section (deep recession): spare capacity means firms can raise output without higher costs. An increase in AD raises real GDP (Y₁ → Y₂) with no rise in the price level.
Upward-sloping section: as the economy nears Yf, bottlenecks and shortages of skilled labour raise costs, so higher AD raises both real GDP and the price level.
Vertical section at Yf: all resources are fully employed, so higher AD only raises the price level (inflation).
examTips: Use this model to argue for fiscal policy in a recession (Keynesian, interventionist view).

diagrams.title: Deflationary (recessionary) gap — new classical model
diagrams.summary: A fall in AD moves short-run equilibrium below potential output, creating cyclical unemployment.
steps: The economy starts in long-run equilibrium at potential output Yp.
A fall in aggregate demand (e.g. falling confidence, higher interest rates, a recession abroad) shifts AD left to AD₂.
Short-run equilibrium moves to e₂: real GDP Y₁ is below potential. The difference is a deflationary (recessionary) gap, with cyclical unemployment and downward pressure on the price level.

diagrams.title: Inflationary gap — new classical model
diagrams.summary: A rise in AD pushes short-run output above potential, creating inflationary pressure.
steps: The economy starts in long-run equilibrium at potential output Yp.
Aggregate demand increases (e.g. a consumption boom or expansionary policy) and AD shifts right to AD₂.

Short-run equilibrium e₂ is beyond potential output: real GDP Y₁ > Yp. This inflationary gap means resources are over-used and the price level rises (demand-pull inflation); unemployment is below its natural rate.

diagrams.title: New classical self-correction of a deflationary gap
diagrams.summary: With flexible wages, falling costs shift SRAS right until the economy returns to potential output.
steps: The economy is in a deflationary gap at e₁: output Y₁ is below potential and unemployment is above the natural rate.
Monetarists/new classical economists argue that wages and prices are flexible. Unemployed workers accept lower wages, and firms' costs fall.
Lower costs shift SRAS right to SRAS₂.
The economy returns to long-run equilibrium at Yp, at a lower price level P₂. Government intervention is unnecessary — and may cause inflation or crowding out.
examTips: Contrast with the Keynesian view that sticky wages can leave the economy stuck in a deflationary gap.

diagrams.title: Keynesian deflationary gap
diagrams.summary: Keynesians argue the economy can stay below full employment for a long time, so the government should raise AD.
steps: Low aggregate demand gives equilibrium at e₁, well below full employment output Yf.

The deflationary gap Yf − Ye means high cyclical unemployment. Because wages are sticky downward and confidence is low, Keynesians argue the economy can remain here — there is no automatic return to Yf.
Expansionary fiscal policy (higher G, lower taxes), boosted by the multiplier, shifts AD right towards Yf. With spare capacity, output rises a lot and the price level only a little.

diagrams.title: Economic growth: LRAS shifts right (new classical)
diagrams.summary: An increase in the quantity or quality of factors of production raises potential output.
steps: Potential output is Yp₁, where LRAS₁ is vertical.
Supply-side improvements — more or better capital, a more skilled workforce, new technology, better institutions — shift LRAS right to LRAS₂.
Potential and actual real GDP can rise to Yp₂ without inflationary pressure; with constant AD the price level would even fall. In practice AD usually grows too.
examTips: This is the macro equivalent of an outward PPC shift.

diagrams.title: Economic growth: Keynesian AS shifts right
diagrams.summary: Supply-side growth shifts the whole Keynesian AS curve right, raising full employment output.
steps: Full employment output is Yf₁.
An increase in the quantity or quality of factors of production (e.g. through interventionist or market-based supply-side policies) shifts AS right to AS₂ and raises full employment output to Yf₂.
With high AD, the shift lowers the price level from P₁ to P₂ and raises real GDP: growth without inflation.

diagrams.title: Demand-pull inflation
diagrams.summary: A rise in AD pulls up the average price level.
steps: The economy is in equilibrium at e₁.
Aggregate demand rises — e.g. rapid consumer credit growth, a rise in government spending, or a boom in export demand — shifting AD right to AD₂.
Firms raise output but, as capacity is approached, costs and prices rise: the price level rises from P₁ to P₂. A sustained rise in AD causes demand-pull inflation.
examTips: Remedies: contractionary monetary or fiscal policy.

diagrams.title: Cost-push inflation (stagflation)
diagrams.summary: Rising costs shift SRAS left: the price level rises while real GDP falls.
steps: The economy is in equilibrium at e₁.
Firms' costs rise — e.g. higher oil prices, higher wages not matched by productivity, a depreciation raising import costs — so SRAS shifts left to SRAS₂.
The price level rises to P₂ while real GDP falls to Y₂ and unemployment rises: stagflation. Policy faces a dilemma — boosting AD worsens inflation; cutting AD deepens the fall in output.

diagrams.title: Structural unemployment in a declining industry
diagrams.summary: A permanent fall in demand for workers with particular skills leaves them unemployed if wages do not fall.
steps: The labour market for a particular industry (e.g. coal mining) is in equilibrium at wage W₁ with Q₁ workers employed.
Demand for the industry's product falls permanently (changing tastes, technology, foreign competition), so demand for its workers falls to DL₂.
If wages do not fall, only Q₂ workers are employed. Those laid off lack the skills or live in the wrong place for jobs elsewhere — a mismatch, so unemployment persists: structural unemployment.
examTips: Remedies are supply-side: retraining, relocation support, better labour market information.

diagrams.title: Short-run Phillips curve
diagrams.summary: In the short run there is a trade-off between inflation and unemployment.
steps: The SRPC shows an inverse relationship between the inflation rate and the unemployment rate.

An increase in AD moves the economy from A to B: more output means less unemployment (U₁ → U₂) but faster inflation (π₁ → π₂), as in an AD/AS diagram where AD shifts right along SRAS. A fall in AD moves the other way.
examTips: A leftward SRAS shift (stagflation) shifts the SRPC up — both inflation and unemployment rise.

diagrams.title: Long-run Phillips curve and the natural rate
diagrams.summary: Expectations adjust, so in the long run unemployment returns to its natural rate at a higher inflation rate.
steps: The economy starts at A: unemployment is at the natural rate (NRU) and inflation is π₁, which people expect to continue.
Expansionary demand-side policy moves the economy along SRPC₁ to B: unemployment falls below the NRU and inflation rises to π₂.

Workers come to expect higher inflation and demand higher wages, so SRAS shifts left and the SRPC shifts up to SRPC₂. Unemployment returns to the NRU at C, with permanently higher inflation. The LRPC is vertical: there is no long-run trade-off.
examTips: The vertical LRPC is the Phillips-curve version of the vertical new classical LRAS.
Only supply-side policies can reduce the NRU (shift the LRPC left).

diagrams.title: Lorenz curve and Gini coefficient
diagrams.summary: The further the Lorenz curve bows away from the line of equality, the more unequal the distribution of income.
steps: The diagonal is the line of perfect equality: every 10% of the population receives 10% of income.
The Lorenz curve shows the actual cumulative share of income received by each cumulative share of the population, from poorest to richest. Here the poorest 50% receive only 18% of income (point a).
The Gini coefficient = area A ÷ (A + B). It ranges from 0 (perfect equality) to 1 (one person has all the income).
A curve further from the diagonal means greater inequality and a higher Gini coefficient. Progressive taxes and transfer payments shift the curve towards the line of equality.

diagrams.title: Money market and expansionary monetary policy
diagrams.summary: The interest rate is set where the demand for money meets the money supply; increasing the money supply lowers it.

elements.text: Lower r → C and I rise → AD shifts right

steps: The demand for money slopes down: the interest rate is the opportunity cost of holding money. The money supply is set by the central bank, so it is vertical. They determine the equilibrium interest rate r₁.

The central bank increases the money supply — buying bonds through open market operations, lowering the minimum reserve requirement, or quantitative easing. Ms shifts right and the interest rate falls to r₂.
Cheaper borrowing raises consumption (especially of durables and housing) and investment, and a lower interest rate tends to depreciate the currency, raising net exports. AD shifts right.
examTips: Evaluation: time lags, weak transmission if confidence is low, and the zero lower bound on interest rates.

diagrams.title: Expansionary fiscal policy and the multiplier
diagrams.summary: Higher government spending shifts AD right; the multiplier makes the final increase in real GDP larger than the initial injection.
steps: The economy is in a deflationary gap at Y₁, well below full employment Yf.
The government raises spending (or cuts taxes). The initial injection shifts AD right by ΔG to AD₂.

That spending becomes income for others, who spend part of it, and so on: the multiplier (1 ÷ (1 − MPC) = 1 ÷ MPW) shifts AD further to AD₃. Real GDP rises to Y₃, closing much of the gap, with only a small rise in the price level because of spare capacity.
examTips: HL: final ΔY = multiplier × ΔG.
Evaluation: crowding out (new classical view), time lags, debt, and inflation if near Yf.

diagrams.title: Comparative advantage and gains from trade
diagrams.summary: Countries gain by specialising in the good with the lower opportunity cost and trading.
steps: Linear PPCs show constant opportunity costs. Country A can produce 80 cloth or 40 wheat; B can produce 30 cloth or 60 wheat.
Opportunity cost of 1 wheat: A gives up 2 cloth, B only ½ cloth. B has the comparative advantage in wheat; A has it in cloth (1 cloth costs A ½ wheat but B 2 wheat).

Each specialises in its comparative-advantage good and they trade at terms between the two opportunity costs — here 1 wheat = 1 cloth. Each country's consumption possibilities now lie along the dashed trading lines.
Both countries can consume combinations outside their own PPC: gains from trade.
examTips: Comparative advantage is about lower OPPORTUNITY COST, not higher output (that is absolute advantage).
Terms of trade must lie between the two countries' opportunity cost ratios.

diagrams.title: Free trade: imports at the world price
diagrams.summary: When the world price is below the domestic equilibrium price, the country imports the difference between domestic consumption and production.
steps: Without trade the domestic market clears at e, price Pd.
With free trade, a small country can import unlimited quantities at the world price Pw: world supply is perfectly elastic.
At Pw, domestic producers supply only Q₁ but consumers buy Q₂. The difference Q₂ − Q₁ is imported.
Consumers gain from lower prices and more choice; domestic producers lose some surplus, but the consumer gain is larger — a net gain in welfare.

diagrams.title: Tariff
diagrams.summary: A tariff raises the domestic price, increases domestic production, cuts consumption and imports, raises revenue and causes welfare loss.
steps: Under free trade the country imports Q₂ − Q₁ at the world price Pw.
A tariff (a tax on imports) raises the price of imports — and so the domestic price — to Pw + tariff.
Domestic production rises to Q₃ and consumption falls to Q₄, so imports shrink to Q₄ − Q₃. Domestic producers gain; consumers lose.
The government earns tariff revenue = tariff × imports.
Two welfare losses: the left triangle is the extra cost of producing Q₁–Q₃ domestically instead of importing more cheaply; the right triangle is the lost consumer surplus from Q₄–Q₂ no longer bought.
examTips: Stakeholders: domestic producers and government gain; consumers and foreign producers lose; the world loses efficiency.

diagrams.title: Import quota
diagrams.summary: A quota limits imports, raising the domestic price; the price gap goes to whoever holds the import licences.
steps: Under free trade the country imports Q₂ − Q₁ at Pw.
A quota allows only a fixed quantity of imports. Above Pw, total supply becomes domestic supply plus the quota.
The domestic price rises to Pq. Domestic production rises to Q₃, consumption falls to Q₄, and imports equal the quota Q₄ − Q₃.
The rectangle is quota rent: the higher price on imported units goes to importers or foreign exporters holding licences — not to the government, unlike tariff revenue.
As with a tariff, the two triangles are welfare losses from inefficient domestic production and reduced consumption.

diagrams.title: Production subsidy as trade protection
diagrams.summary: A subsidy to domestic producers raises domestic output and cuts imports without changing the price consumers pay.
steps: Under free trade domestic firms produce Q₁, consumers buy Q₃ at Pw, and imports are Q₃ − Q₁.
The government pays domestic producers a subsidy per unit, shifting domestic supply down.
At the unchanged world price, domestic production rises to Q₂, so imports fall to Q₃ − Q₂. Consumers pay Pw as before.
The government pays subsidy × Q₂. The triangle is a welfare loss: the subsidised units cost more to produce domestically than to import.
examTips: Consumers are not directly affected — only taxpayers, domestic producers and foreign exporters.

diagrams.title: Floating exchange rate determination
diagrams.summary: The exchange rate is set by the demand for and supply of the currency on the foreign exchange market.
steps: The y axis is the price of this currency in terms of another (e.g. US$ per €). Equilibrium is where quantity demanded equals quantity supplied.
Demand comes from foreigners who need the currency to buy the country's exports and assets; supply comes from residents selling it to buy imports and foreign assets.

diagrams.title: Appreciation from an increase in demand for the currency
diagrams.summary: Higher demand for a currency raises its value.
steps: The currency is initially at ER₁.
Demand for the currency rises — e.g. higher relative interest rates attract hot money, export demand grows, inward FDI rises, or speculators expect appreciation.
The currency appreciates to ER₂. Exports become dearer abroad and imports cheaper: a risk to the current account and to export industries, but lower imported inflation.

diagrams.title: Depreciation from an increase in supply of the currency
diagrams.summary: Higher supply of a currency lowers its value.
steps: The currency is initially at ER₁.
Supply of the currency rises — e.g. residents buy more imports, domestic firms invest abroad, interest rates fall relative to other countries, or higher inflation makes exports less competitive.
The currency depreciates to ER₂. Exports become cheaper abroad and imports dearer, which can improve the current account (if the Marshall–Lerner condition holds) but adds to cost-push inflation.

diagrams.title: Maintaining a fixed exchange rate
diagrams.summary: When market forces push the currency below its peg, the central bank buys its own currency to hold the rate.
steps: The government fixes the currency at the rate shown, which initially is also the market equilibrium.
Supply of the currency rises to S₂ (e.g. imports increase). At the fixed rate there is now excess supply, which would push the currency down.

The central bank buys its own currency using foreign currency reserves (and/or raises interest rates to attract financial inflows), shifting demand to D₂ so the rate stays at the peg. This cannot continue if reserves run out — then the currency may have to be devalued.

diagrams.title: The J-curve effect
diagrams.summary: After a depreciation the current account first worsens, then improves once demand becomes more price elastic.
steps: The country has a current account deficit (below the zero line).
The currency depreciates (or is devalued), making exports cheaper abroad and imports dearer.
In the short run, contracts are fixed and buyers take time to switch, so demand for exports and imports is price inelastic. The country pays more for roughly the same imports: the deficit gets worse.

Over time demand becomes more elastic. Once the Marshall–Lerner condition holds (PEDx + PEDm > 1), export revenue rises relative to import spending and the current account improves — tracing a J shape.

diagrams.title: The poverty cycle (trap)
diagrams.summary: Low incomes lead to low saving and investment, which keep productivity and incomes low.
steps: Low incomes leave little to save after meeting basic needs, so there are few funds for investment. Low investment in physical and human capital keeps productivity low, so incomes stay low — the cycle repeats and can pass between generations.

Escaping the trap needs an injection from outside the cycle: foreign aid, FDI, microfinance, public investment in education, health and infrastructure, debt relief, or better access to markets (e.g. fair trade).
